title: Catching the ox
hookLine: fourth picture: he catches it, and it fights the rope

lines: IT THROWS ITS HEAD AND BOLTS.
cards: What comes after a breakthrough? Stories about change usually stop at the moment of insight: the light comes on, the music swells, the credits roll. The oxherding pictures keep going.
In the fourth picture the herdsman finally gets a rope around the ox. And the ox is not grateful to be found. It throws its head, it bolts, it drags him toward the hills.
The rope goes taut in his hands.

teach.h: AT LAST, THE OX ON A ROPE.
teach.b: First, at last, the ox on a rope. After searching, tracks and a glimpse, the thing he's been looking for is no longer out in the grass. It's in his hands.

teach.h: LONG IN THE WILD, STILL WILD.
teach.b: Second, it's still wild. The preface, in paraphrase, says the ox has lived so long in the wilderness that it's hard to hold. It still longs for the sweet grass; its stubborn streak is still strong.

Being caught doesn't erase the habits of all those years. A clear moment doesn't come with new reflexes. The old pulls are there the next morning: the scroll, the snap at someone you love, the worry that circles at night.

teach.h: IT PULLS HARD. THAT'S WHAT OXEN DO.
teach.b: Third, it pulls hard. The verse has him holding on with all his strength while the ox charges toward the high ground or drifts off into misty valleys. The picture doesn't scold the ox.
A wild ox pulls. The struggle isn't a sign the glimpse was fake; it's what holding on looks like at first.

The preface says that to make the ox gentle, he'll need the whip. Some readers hear that as firmness, not cruelty: steady effort and attention, returning again and again. The fourth picture is the stage of grip.
Tomorrow's is the stage of patience.

how: Zen teachers often point to the fourth oxherding picture when students find that old habits return after a clear moment in practice, treating the struggle as a normal stage that calls for steady effort.

o: giving up the search because the ox is far too wild
the moment the wild ox is trapped and can never wander
holding on as old habits pull hard, after a real glimpse

games.q: catching the ox: tap the pairs.
p: he finally has hold of the ox
why the ox is hard to hold
what the ox still longs for

the fourth picture shows the ox fighting the rope; taming comes next.

games.q: you've got the rope on the ox at last. it bolts for the hills and drags you with it. what does the fourth picture show the herdsman doing?
o: letting go: it was never meant to be caught.
holding on with all his strength.
deciding he never really saw it.
games.why: the verse has him holding on with everything he has while the ox charges and wanders. the struggle is part of the path, not proof he failed.

practice: Rest with the breath, and before long something will pull: an itch, a plan, a replayed argument, the urge to check the time.

Don't fight it and don't follow it; stay with it, the way the herdsman stays on the rope, and feel exactly where it tugs, in the hands, the chest, the jaw. Then come back to the breath, and when it pulls again, stay again.

wordCard.voice: Catching the ox. The fourth oxherding picture: the herdsman gets the ox on a rope, and the ox, long wild, fights it. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (deniu): 'getting the ox', the name of the fourth oxherding picture.

carryVoice: Your line: it pulls. That's simply what a wild ox does. Rope in hand, see you tomorrow.
